facts.text: Commissioned for the Munich court carnival. Nothing says party season like a vow to sacrifice your son.
facts.evidence: Mozart and Varesco were commissioned in 1780 by Karl Theodor, Elector of Bavaria for a court carnival.
facts.plain: Idomeneo was a commission: in 1780 the Elector of Bavaria, Karl Theodor, asked Mozart and librettist Varesco for an opera for the Munich court carnival.

facts.text: That soft “ending” is a fake-out: the chords slide straight into G minor for Ilia’s first scene.
facts.evidence: turn out not to be a resolution of the overture in the tonic but chords in the dominant of G minor
facts.plain: Listen to the end of the overture: its soft final chords are not a real ending but lead straight into G minor, the key of Ilia’s opening scene.

facts.text: Opening night: 29 January 1781, Cuvilliés Theatre, Munich. Conductor: Christian Cannabich.
evidence: It was first performed at the Cuvilliés Theatre of the Munich Residenz on 29 January 1781, under the musical direction of Christian Cannabich.
facts.plain: The opera premiered on 29 January 1781 at the Cuvilliés Theatre in Munich, conducted by Christian Cannabich.

facts.text: The Munich press raved about the scenery — the port, Neptune’s temple — and never named Mozart.
evidence: a notice in the Munich press did not mention Mozart by name
the view of the port and Neptune's temple were outstanding
facts.plain: The Munich press notice of the premiere didn’t mention Mozart by name. It raved about the sets instead, especially the view of the port and Neptune’s temple.

facts.text: Idamante was written for a castrato. Five years later Mozart rewrote him as a tenor. Opera puberty.
evidence: A concert performance was given in 1786 at the Palais Auersperg in Vienna.
changed Idamante from a castrato to a tenor
facts.plain: Idamante was written for a castrato. For a 1786 concert performance in Vienna, Mozart rewrote the part for a tenor.

facts.text: The singers objected to vowels. Too many i’s in “rinvigorir”, so Mozart changed the words.
facts.evidence: Mozart fought with the librettist, the court chaplain Varesco, making large cuts and changes, even down to specific words and vowels disliked by the singers
facts.plain: Mozart fought with his librettist, the court chaplain Varesco, making big cuts and even changing words whose vowels the singers disliked, like the many i’s in “rinvigorir”.

facts.text: Elettra is jealous of Ilia, so she summons the furies of the underworld. Proportionate.
facts.evidence: feels the furies of the underworld rise up in her heart
facts.plain: Elettra’s “Tutte nel cor vi sento”: jealous of Ilia, she feels the furies of the underworld rising up in her heart.

facts.text: This shipwreck follows Gluck’s storm scene in Iphigénie en Tauride almost beat for beat.
facts.evidence: the shipwreck scene towards the end of act 1 is almost identical to the structure and dramatic working-out of a similar scene in Gluck's Iphigénie en Tauride
facts.plain: This shipwreck scene closely follows the structure of a similar storm scene in Gluck’s Iphigénie en Tauride.

facts.text: The vow: sacrifice the first living creature he meets on land. Guess who shows up first. (His son.)
facts.evidence: to sacrifice, if he should arrive safely on land, the first living creature he should meet
facts.plain: Saved from the storm, Idomeneo remembers his vow to Neptune: to sacrifice the first living creature he meets on land. It will be his own son.

facts.text: Anton Raaff, the first Idomeneo, never played another stage role. Retired on a shipwreck.
evidence: Raaff sang the title role in the premiere of Mozart's 1781 opera Idomeneo; this was his last stage role.
facts.plain: Mozart wrote the title role for the tenor Anton Raaff, who sang it at the 1781 premiere. It was Raaff’s last stage role.

facts.text: Critic Schubart called Raaff’s voice the most beautiful male voice of all time. No pressure, tonight’s tenor.
facts.attribution: C. F. D. Schubart (via Wikipedia, “Anton Raaff”)
facts.evidence: In the opinion of Schubart, his was the most beautiful male voice of all time
facts.plain: The critic Schubart thought Anton Raaff, the first Idomeneo, had the most beautiful male voice of all time.

facts.text: The troops come home, the wives meet the boat, everyone thanks Neptune. Nobody mentions the vow.
facts.evidence: In an intermezzo between acts 1 and 2, Cretan troops disembarking from Idomeneo's ship are met by their wives, and all praise Neptune.
facts.plain: In this intermezzo between Acts I and II, Cretan troops come off Idomeneo’s ship, their wives meet them, and everyone praises Neptune.

facts.text: Hear the piccolo? Enjoy it. This Act II storm is the only place Mozart uses it.
facts.evidence: piccolo (only in the storm of act 2)
facts.plain: Mozart saves the piccolo for this one place in the opera: the storm in Act II.

facts.text: Ilia asks the breezes to carry her love to Idamante. Long-distance messaging, 1781 edition.
facts.evidence: Ilia asks the breezes to carry her love to Idamante
facts.plain: “Zeffiretti lusinghieri”: alone in the royal garden, Ilia asks the breezes to carry her love to Idamante.

facts.text: The three trombones play nowhere else in the opera. When a god speaks, you bring brass.
facts.evidence: 3 trombones (only accompanying the off-stage voice of Neptune in act 3)
facts.plain: The three trombones play only here, to accompany the offstage Voice of Neptune.

facts.text: Ends in the overture’s key: a first for Mozart, and a habit in every opera he wrote after.
facts.evidence: ended the work in the key of the overture
facts.plain: Idomeneo was the first opera in which Mozart ended in the key of the overture, and he did so in all his later operas.

facts.text: All that work, all those fights with the librettist… Munich performed it three times.
facts.evidence: Idomeneo was performed three times in Munich.
facts.plain: Despite all that work, Idomeneo was performed only three times in Munich.

facts.text: Munich’s management also wanted a ballet. Mozart delivered about 15 minutes of dances. Bonus track: K. 367.
evidence: he reported in a letter to his father of 30 December 1780
It is in several parts and lasts around fifteen minutes.
facts.plain: Mozart also wrote about 15 minutes of ballet music (K. 367) for Idomeneo, which the Munich management requested. He reported on it in a letter to his father on 30 December 1780.

facts.text: Later in 1781 Mozart considered a Gluck-style redo: bass Idomeneo, tenor Idamante. Never happened.
facts.evidence: this would have meant a bass Idomeneo and a tenor Idamante
facts.plain: Later in 1781 Mozart considered making the opera more like Gluck, with a bass Idomeneo and a tenor Idamante, but he never did.

facts.text: 1931: Richard Strauss “updated” Idomeneo, swapping about a third of Mozart’s music for his own.
evidence: the Vienna State Opera presented a distinctively interventionist version of the score by Richard Strauss
Strauss replaced about 1/3 of Mozart's score with some of his own music
facts.plain: For the 150th anniversary in 1931, Richard Strauss made his own version for Vienna, replacing about a third of Mozart’s score with his own music.

facts.text: America’s first Idomeneo: Tanglewood, 1947. Only 166 years after the premiere.
facts.evidence: The first performance in the United States was produced by Boris Goldovsky at the Berkshire Music Festival at Tanglewood during the summer of 1947.
facts.plain: The first US performance came only in 1947, at Tanglewood, produced by Boris Goldovsky.

facts.text: Berlin’s Deutsche Oper cancelled an Idomeneo revival over an added final scene, citing an “incalculable security risk”.
evidence: the Deutsche Oper Berlin announced the cancellation of four performances
incalculable security risk
facts.plain: In 2006 the Deutsche Oper Berlin cancelled a revival of Hans Neuenfels’s Idomeneo, citing an “incalculable security risk” over its added final scene.

facts.text: This Ponnelle staging was the Met’s first Idomeneo ever, in 1982: 201 years after the premiere. Pavarotti sang the king.
facts.attribution: Met Opera Archives, performance record CID 270240
evidence: Metropolitan Opera Premiere, New Production
Thu, October 14, 1982
Idomeneo Luciano Pavarotti
Production Jean-Pierre Ponnelle
facts.plain: This Jean-Pierre Ponnelle staging was the Met’s first production of Idomeneo. It opened on October 14, 1982, with Luciano Pavarotti in the title role.

facts.text: The Ponnelle look: Roman columns, a grand staircase, Piranesi-style ruins. Crete, via Rome.
facts.attribution: F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
evidence: Ponnelle's use of classical Roman columns framing the stage, a broad flight of steps between
all clearly derived from Piranesi
facts.plain: Ponnelle framed the stage with classical Roman columns and a broad flight of steps, in front of changing backdrops of ruins inspired by Piranesi.

facts.text: 1982: Hildegard Behrens’s Elettra “literally stopped the show” with this aria, said one critic.
facts.attribution: F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
facts.evidence: Hildegard Behrens as Elettra, thrwarted in her efforts to win Idamante from Ilia, literally stopped the show with her brilliant last act aria
facts.plain: At the Met premiere, a critic wrote that Hildegard Behrens as Elettra “literally stopped the show” with this last-act aria.

facts.text: A 1982 critic called these perhaps the first realistic musical tempests in any opera. Umbrellas up.
facts.attribution: F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
evidence: two magnificent sequences of storm music, thought bo be the first such realistic musical tempests in any opera
facts.plain: The 1982 Washington Times review praised the opera’s two storm sequences, which it called perhaps the first realistic musical tempests in any opera.

facts.text: Welcome to Sidon, a port city of Crete. Population: zero. It’s fictional.
evidence: At the port of Sidon (a fictional city of Crete)

facts.text: Neptune’s reply to a dodged vow: a storm AND a sea serpent. Gods don’t do refunds.
evidence: a storm breaks out, and a sea serpent appears

facts.text: The big monster fight? Offstage. Arbace just walks in and reports that Idamante killed it.
evidence: Arbace brings news that Idamante has killed the monster

facts.text: Happy ending! Everyone is relieved… except Elettra, who longs for her own death.
evidence: Everyone is relieved except Electra, who longs for her own death.

facts.text: 1931: houses feared Idomeneo was “hopelessly unstageworthy”. Fix: two remixes, by Wolf-Ferrari and Strauss.
evidence: hopelessly unstageworthy
Munich commissioned an Idomeneo revision from Ermanno Wolf-Ferrari, performed in 1931
the Vienna State Opera presented a distinctively interventionist version of the score by Richard Strauss

facts.text: Britain’s first Idomeneo, 1934, wasn’t at a big opera house. It was the amateur Glasgow Grand Opera Society.
evidence: The British premiere was given by the amateur Glasgow Grand Opera Society under Erik Chisholm on 12 March 1934.

facts.text: 1993: a 50-minute kids’ Idomeneo, with one actor playing almost every role. Quick changes.
evidence: 50-minute version for children, with actor Frank Groothof playing almost all roles

facts.text: Mozart and his first Idomeneo got their own opera, RAAFF. Its orchestra includes a Fender Rhodes and a drum kit.
evidence: centers around the problematic relationship and friendship between young Mozart and the much older Anton Raaff
including a fretless bass guitar, a Fender Rhodes and a drum kit
